content:
Mexico has met the minimum annual water delivery to the United States under the 1944 Water Treaty, delivering at least 350,000 acre-feet — about 431 million cubic meters — from the Río Bravo in the first year of the treaty's Cycle 37, according to Mexico's Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE).

The SRE confirmed the milestone on October 24, the end of the cycle's first year, which runs from October 2025 to October 2030. The ministry said the delivery was achieved in a context of extreme drought, through interagency efforts under joint strategies announced on February 3, 2026, and without putting at risk the human right to water, community consumption, or food production in the border region.

U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins confirmed the delivery in a message on X, saying Mexico met its commitment for the year, while warning that the work is not over: continued deliveries and repayment of the outstanding water debt remain critical for farmers and ranchers in South Texas, according to reports of her message.

The milestone follows a tense chapter in the treaty dispute. Last year, President Donald Trump twice accused Mexico of violating the 1944 treaty and demanded immediate delivery under threat of tariffs, according to La Jornada's report on the SRE announcement. Mexico's ambassador to the United States, Roberto Lazzeri, framed the delivery as the product of dialogue and bilateral cooperation, guided by mutual respect, sovereignty, and shared responsibility.

Under the treaty framework, Mexico is to deliver 1.75 million acre-feet over each five-year cycle, with the 350,000 acre-foot figure as the annual minimum. The February 2026 agreement also included a plan to repay the debt accumulated during the previous cycle, which U.S. officials have described as a priority for Texas agriculture.

What to watch next: whether Mexico keeps pace with the annual minimum in the remaining years of Cycle 37, how the outstanding debt is repaid, and what the deliveries mean for river levels and South Texas farms and ranches that depend on Río Bravo water.

Sources: Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE), as reported by La Jornada, October 24, 2026; U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, message on X, as reported October 25, 2026.

title: Mexico meets annual Río Bravo water delivery to the U.S. despite extreme drought
